title: Discovering and Steering Interpretable Concepts in Large Generative Music Models
claim: A staged pipeline extracts model activations, learns sparse features, filters them, and labels them automatically, with the same features usable for steering.
layout: 3 numbered panels, left-to-right, dashed dividers, feedback loop for steering
description: A wide three-stage diagram with numbered circular headers separated by dashed vertical lines. Stage 1, Activation Extraction: a music corpus (notes and a clef) feeds a stacked-layer icon, then a bar-style transformer model labeled as a music generation model (e.g. MusicGen). Gray lines fan out from the layers to four colorful activation-map stacks, the residual stream activation dataset. Stage 2, Unsupervised Feature Discovery: a sparse autoencoder drawn as black Enc and Dec trapezoids around a dark grid of dots, the sparse feature matrix. A reconstruction-loss formula sits above a gray loop. Below, a filtering step leads to rows marked with red crosses or green checks. Green lines run to two knobs labeled Steering. Stage 3, Automatic Labeling: maximally activating example waveforms in teal, orange and navy, then generative labeling (a G box with a schema) and classifier-based labeling, ending in spectrogram examples labeled Drum Roll and Silence. Bold arrows carry the flow, and the dark SAE block draws the eye first.
caption: Multi-stage pipeline for discovering and steering interpretable concepts in autoregressive music models. (1) Music from a large corpus is passed through a pre-trained generator to extract activations from multiple layers. (2) Sparse autoencoders reconstruct activations (also usable for steering), and features are filtered to retain the most viable candidates. (3) Retained features are characterized via musical examples and labeled using generative labeling with a multimodal LM and classifier-based labeling with pre-trained models.
abstract: The fidelity with which neural networks can now generate content such as music presents a scientific opportunity: these systems appear to have learned implicit theories of such content's structure through statistical learning alone. This offers a potentially new lens on theories of human-generated media. When internal representations align with traditional constructs (e.g. chord progressions in music), they show how such categories can emerge from statistical regularities; when they diverge, they expose limits of existing frameworks and patterns we may have overlooked but that nonetheless carry explanatory power. In this paper, focusing on autoregressive music generators, we introduce a method for discovering interpretable concepts using sparse autoencoders (SAEs), extracting interpretable features from the residual stream of a transformer model. We make this approach scalable and evaluable using automated labeling and validation pipelines. Our results reveal both familiar musical concepts and coherent but uncodified patterns lacking clear counterparts in theory or language. As an extension, we show such concepts can be used to steer model generations. Beyond improving model transparency, our work provides an empirical tool for uncovering organizing principles that have eluded traditional methods of analysis and synthesis.
